Karoo Drought - Humanitarian Disaster

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
The rains came for the rest of the drought stricken country but in the central Karoo, Carnarvon, Williston Sutherland the main sheep producing areas its been 7 long dry years. They got 3 months of drought relief in 2018 but the rains never came and the farmers cant go on. The biggest causality are the farm workers, half have been laid off. Emerging farmers can't afford to employ anyone permanently and rely on causal workers when they have enough money to employ them. People are surviving on SASA grants and soup kitchens. Kids are turning to crime and dropping out of school with drug and alcohol abuse is rife

Summary:
In many parts of the country the drought has broken- the horrific images of the Free State KZN that haunted our lives- these farmers have had rain. But the area in the central Karoo around Carnarvon, Sutherland and Williston they are into their 7th year of drought. Sheep numbers decreased by 11 870, and average weaning percentage by 27%. The average feed bill per month is R52 461. The sheep are dying, the ewes are not lambing and the farmers are slaughtering their breeding stock because they can’t afford to feed them. The price of red meat has dropped by R10 kilogram n effect on a 20kg carcass the producer gets nearly R200 less per lamb. 12 000 less sheep from 26 farmers equals R2,4million loss. They have been waiting for over a year to get assistance from the State despite the area having been declared a disaster area in 2018.

Further information:
There are 30 emerging farmers in the Carnarvon area and they are really battling. They rent land from the Municipality and they can’t afford the rent because productivity is down. Dirk Saccoo head of the Emerging Farmers Assocaition used to have 1000 sheep he now has 200. They can’t afford to employ people on a fulltime basis anymore so only take casual labour when they need something fixed. They can’t fix the fences because they don’t have money and the jackals are attacking and killing the sheep. They can’t get credit at the Agri Co-Op for feed or from the banks.

They are also victim to stock left. Dirk is also on the security council so can speak to the other farmers problems. He cannot afford the petrol to drive to his farm which is 140 kms out of town- he used to make the trip twice a week now barley gets their once a week. The farm workers that are still on the farms are having to do everything on their own from repairing fences to feeding the sheep to fixing the windmills. The farmers can’t afford the fuel to travel back and forth so they have to survive longer and longer on their own managing the farms.

Essentially it’s a humanitarian crisis- farmers are just not employing people on the farms- out of the 150 farms that would cover 300 families and on every farm they have has lost either 1 or 2 workers and when you consider they only employ 3 or 4 people that a huge impact. Usually farmers also used 6 casual workers on a day for big work, now they take only 2. There is no money for additional work like fence maintenance. Side line industries are failing and the people they employ.

For example Sybrand Venter used to run a sideline business of scanning pregnant ewes he used to scan 35 000 ewes now if he scans 1000 it’s a lot.

Danie Franken manager of the local Abattoir in Carnarvon says they employed 89 people- they are the largest employer in town. The number of sheep that are being slaughtered has fallen so dramatically that they are only working 4 days a week instead of 5. The abattoir used to slaughter 175 000 sheep in normal years, last year it’s down to 100 000, the expectation for this year is 80 000. They recently retrenched 10 workers and no longer employ casual workers- so 35 people have lost work. Each person supports on average 4 people so the impact here is on 140 people. In Williston they are already working short time so people are earning 80% of their wages

Lamb sales are down by 50% because the economy is so bad as a result the price of red meat per kg has dropped by R10 kg so R200 less for every sheep. Imported lanb is selling at R37kg which the local market can just not compete against

The farmers are slaughtering replacement ewes and even pregnant ewes just to survive. This means even if they do get some rain it will be a number of years before the stock can increase.

The Local Spar and DIY and garage is owned by Heinz Germann- he reports an 42% drop in their turn over- farmers and workers cannot afford any treats or luxuries they are buying the essential. They used to employ 86 people between the 3 businesses and now only 50 people- 30 people have lost their jobs impacting 120 people. But all expenses have increased- Rates, electricity and insurance.

50% of the workers are now unemployed so people with young children are surviving on SASA grants from their kids. Many workers already returned to town when they lost their jobs on the farms that were bought up around SKA – this number has increased over the last few years- this is visually evident with the growing numbers of workers gathering in town on a Monday looking for casual work

The social worker off the record says there is a growing problem with the kids, increasing housebreaking, drug and alcohol abuse, the children are neglected. For example she is dealing with an 11 years girl who old broke into a house and stole stuff. There is an increasing in crime and rape, with a growing problem of drug abuse but there has always been a problem of alcohol abuse.

The school principle of the junior school - Vanessa Vyfer will go on camera- she says for many of the kids the only meal they eat is the one they get at school. The kids that used to stay in the hostel have moved out now that their parents are back in town, which she can’t understand because it’s not because of financial problems, they only pay R50 and if they can’t afford it she does make them pay. Sometimes they run a soup kitchen for the community when they have extra food and she says the queues of starving people is hectic.

Willem Symington -Vice Chairman Agri Northern Cape. He works with the 3 spheres of Government to get drought relief, he is very articulate and comfortable speaking English and has a very good grip on where the blocks of access to funding lie. They have been trying to get funding since last July and with elections and new people appointed to positions basically every just stopped working until the new people were in place.

In August this year they finally declared the area a disaster but it has to be registered in the Government gazette and it’s now September and that has not happened and the concern is that money has to be released within 3 months. The bigger picture is the agricultural disasters used to be handled by the DAFF but they are no longer- all disasters whether floods or drought are now handled by Co-operative governance, traditional affairs and Human Settlement- COGTHS- essentially it’s a mess and he spends his life traveling to Kimberly or De Aar to handle the various layers of Government to unlock the funding.


Extra Budget Items:
Carnarvon is a 4 hour drive from Kimberley and then the farms are outside Carnarvon so approximately 10 hours of our 2 shoot days will be spent travelling. The flights are expensive so in order to get the content and quality images to justify the expense of the flights it makes sense to fly in on the Sunday evening. We also need a car with high clearance as we will be travelling on farm roads

Script:


Script: When you drive through the vast arid landscape of the Karoo, you would be forgiven for thinking it’s in a permanent state of drought. Farmers here are used to weathering them when they last a couple of years, but this drought is going into its 7th year. There is nothing left in the veld for the sheep to eat, and now 70% of the Northern Cape is gripped in a disastrous drought, one of the worst in more than a century, and farmers can no longer cope on their own.
Willem“When it was a national drought. It was big news but all those areas have received some relief but the Northern Cape haven't received that relief as far as rain is concerned. In fact the situation has worsened and it almost feels as if we in the Northern Cape has become a forgotten drought.
Script: Willem Symington farms in Williston, but as Vice President of Agri Northern Cape he spends most of his time driving across the Karoo attending meetings, trying to alert the authorities to this humanitarian disaster
Link “ Most farmers have had to sell half their sheep and the money they have made on that they have spent on feed keeping the rest of the flock alive, they have run out of credit, used up their life savings and re bonded their farms
Dirk” When we talk about the drought, it always brings a lump into the throat because it affected us so badly
Script : Emerging farmer Dirk Sacco used to win regional awards for his quality sheep, now he’s cut back on his own meals to keep them alive. His grandfather was a farmer so it’s in his blood, but as head of the emerging farmers, he feels the state has forgotten them
Dirk “We can’t breed lambs anymore and now they are being stolen as well, some people have lost hope and they have left, but if it is in your heart then you won’t drop it and leave
Script : With a 30% drop in the price of meat, they are farming at a loss says Sybrand Venter, Vice Chairman of Agri Kareeberg.
Sybrand “At the moment everyone is desperate just to stay alive I think. The old farmers who have been farming for 30, 40 years they are beginning to use their retirement money just to keep the farms going. The young guys are talking about closing their gates and going to look for work. So the need is very big
Script : Dirk lives with his family in town and rents his farmland from the Municipality. His biggest fear, is that he will be evicted if he can’t pay the annual farm rental
Dirk “As a renter, I don’t have property rights and I don’t have access to capital from the bank because I have no security, what I’ve got left now is debt, We know that sooner or later the bank will say to us, that’s far enough.
Script”The knock on effect of the drought in this region is about R3.8 billion to the economy as a whole. 60 000 people in this area have lost their jobs because these rural economies are dependent on the farmers, when they go down, the whole community goes down with them, keeping the sheep alive, keeps the town alive
Sybrand ” there is a reduction of up to 40% unemployment among the permanent farm workers. The casual workers, the guys are using 50% fewer occasional workers and there is no money to pay workers
Dirt “; The government had a slogan, “a better life for all”, and for me it is getting even worse, you no longer know how you are going to tell your wife what can be on the table tomorrow . At my age I have to go and work as a casual (labourer) at the quarry, not just to feed my sheep, but also to keep my household going.
Script There is a growing number of unemployed men gathering on the street corners, hoping a farmer will pick them up but as the drought bites harder the work becomes more scarce
Sampie Jors “ It’s mostly casual jobs unloading lorries with drought feed it’s the only jobs we get in this town. Many of the farmers first have to feed their animals and far fewer people are on the farms
Albert Jood “I look for casual work every day, it pays R150, R120 a day”
Sybrand “If you stop the bakkie and you just want to pick up two people, your bakkie is stormed by 15 , 20 people but you can only take two. You know 5 or 6 of the men because you have worked with them a lot and you can see the men are having a hard time but you can only take two
Script : Vanessa Pheiffer Principle of Carnarvon Primary school, says their school feeding scheme supports 1280 learners, and between Williston Sutherland and Carnarvon, nearly 5 thousand children depend on this meal to survive.
Vanessa “Many families had to move from farms to come and live in Carnarvon under difficult circumstances some are squatting with families.
Link “ For some of these children this is the only meal that they will have today the weekends are tough because their families are living off the state grants which is only about R400 per child
Vanessa “ We have a 95 per cent learner presence at the school, they come because the meal is actually at school.
Script: The impact on the farm children whose parents have lost their jobs is particularly heart wrenching, says Maths teacher Benjamin Hoorn
Benjamin ” You can see it from children that when they are at the farm, the farm owner supplied everything you will see that the children is very well well dressed.These people were used to staying in a house and then suddenly they must move into a squatter camp, in the farms they have the facilities that you don't get in the towns
Link “This general dealer behind me has seen a 42% drop in turnover in the last year that’s the worst he has ever seen in 26 years of operation. The farmers are spending so much money on feed they can barely afford food for their families and their staff
Hein “the farmers owe us money, they're not getting the money because the price on sheep is falling,the price on the wool is falling.
Script : Heinz Germann owner of the general dealer and hardware says most farmers are just buying to stay alive
Heinz” When the farmers come to buy their own groceries they even walk off behind their wives to just check that there's no fancy stuff going into that basket it's only necessities. There's nothing else selling.
Script : Heinz has also had to drastically cut down on staff
Heinz” We had we had more than 30 workers we got less than 18 now
Script” Canravon abattoir employs the largest number of people in town, and is a very good barometer of how bad things are, with a 39% drop in sheep being slaughtered, they’ve retrenched 35 workers, and in Williston they working 4 day weeks
Link “ This area last received government assistance about a year ago but the rain has still not come and if aid doesn’t arrive soon there is a danger that this rural community will collapse
Willem “We received 127 million for one district in 2018 and it provided immense relief. But it's been more than a year since the government has done anything to mitigate the effects of this drought
Script ”The longer it takes, the more the national breeding herd is being depleted
Sybrand” If the government had helped,you would have stayed in production, and then people could have carried on and kept their workers and insurance the government should have come in in 2016 and taken this thing and driven it, but we are standing here 3 years later almost without any help
Script” In terms of the drought disaster legislation, first the district municipalities and then the province have to declare it a disaster and gazette it, before it can be escalated to the national disaster management centre who appeal to Treasury
Willem “ While this 127 million was being spent last year we started motivating and requesting further financial support for this area.
Script” The declaration is for 3 months and then it must be renewed on a monthly basis, ideally until the drought ends. The Department of Agriculture estimates R450 million rand is needed for the first 3 months and its likely to escalate to R600 million. The fundamental problem is droughts are not finite, they require an open ended budget, until the rains come and the veld recovers, and that’s not happening
Claire “Has the premier of the Northern Cape declared this a disaster area.
Willem ” We as organised agriculture had a meeting with the Premier in the end of July 2019 and we made presentations to him. He listened to us he gave us a good ear...and since then nothing has happened.
Claire “Nothing.
Willem “ We haven't seen a provincial declaration and we haven't seen any aid yet
Script” Finally on Friday deputy president David Mabusa visited the region and agreed the situation is dire.
“National Government as well as the province will try and cooperate pull hands together and help the farmers
Script “Committing to R30 million for immediate relief, with more to follow.
Over the past year the Department of Agriculture has assisted with fodder where they could, but what keeps farmers spirits up are donations from the public
Sybrand ” there are people who do huge work people like radio Tygerberg gave us a bunch of loads of of feed and on one day we could give 163 farmers each a bakkie of feed. So rain doesn’t always come out of the sky, rain sometimes comes down the tarred road as well
Link “Even if it rained today and the drought relief funding arrived it would still take another five years for this community to begin to recover
Sybrand ”To recover economically - You’re talking about long term loans people have taken on. It will take 10, 15, some guys 20 years just to work off that debt. But you have to go on because it’s in our blood, it’s our life, we just have to hang in there and to hope and believe
Dirk “ My spirituality says to hold out, because I think God is aware of what is happening and we still believe there will be a solution.

Script There is a growing number of unemployed men gathering on the street corners, hoping a farmer will pick them up but as the drought bites harder the work becomes more scarce Sampie Jors “ It’s mostly casual jobs unloading lorries with drought feed it’s the only jobs we get in this town. Many of the farmers first have to feed their animals and far fewer people are on the farms Albert Jood “I look for casual work every day, it pays R150, R120 a day” Sybrand “If you stop the bakkie and you just want to pick up two people, your bakkie is stormed by 15 , 20 people but you can only take two. You know 5 or 6 of the men because you have worked with them a lot and you can see the men are having a hard time but you can only take two Script : Vanessa Pheiffer Principle of Carnarvon Primary school, says their school feeding scheme supports 1280 learners, and between Williston Sutherland and Carnarvon, nearly 5 thousand children depend on this meal to survive. Vanessa “Many families had to move from farms to come and live in Carnarvon under difficult circumstances some are squatting with families. Link “ For some of these children this is the only meal that they will have today the weekends are tough because their families are living off the state grants which is only about R400 per child Vanessa “ We have a 95 per cent learner presence at the school, they come because the meal is actually at school. Script: The impact on the farm children whose parents have lost their jobs is particularly heart wrenching, says Maths teacher Benjamin Hoorn Benjamin ” You can see it from children that when they are at the farm, the farm owner supplied everything you will see that the children is very well well dressed.These people were used to staying in a house and then suddenly they must move into a squatter camp, in the farms they have the facilities that you don't get in the towns Link “This general dealer behind me has seen a 42% drop in turnover in the last year that’s the worst he has ever seen in 26 years of operation. The farmers are spending so much money on feed they can barely afford food for their families and their staff Hein “the farmers owe us money, they're not getting the money because the price on sheep is falling,the price on the wool is falling. Script : Heinz Germann owner of the general dealer and hardware says most farmers are just buying to stay alive Heinz” When the farmers come to buy their own groceries they even walk off behind their wives to just check that there's no fancy stuff going into that basket it's only necessities. There's nothing else selling. Script : Heinz has also had to drastically cut down on staff Heinz” We had we had more than 30 workers we got less than 18 now Script” Canravon abattoir employs the largest number of people in town, and is a very good barometer of how bad things are, with a 39% drop in sheep being slaughtered, they’ve retrenched 35 workers, and in Williston they working 4 day weeks Link “ This area last received government assistance about a year ago but the rain has still not come and if aid doesn’t arrive soon there is a danger that this rural community will collapse Willem “We received 127 million for one district in 2018 and it provided immense relief. But it's been more than a year since the government has done anything to mitigate the effects of this drought Script ”The longer it takes, the more the national breeding herd is being depleted Sybrand” If the government had helped,you would have stayed in production, and then people could have carried on and kept their workers and insurance the government should have come in in 2016 and taken this thing and driven it, but we are standing here 3 years later almost without any help Script” In terms of the drought disaster legislation, first the district municipalities and then the province have to declare it a disaster and gazette it, before it can be escalated to the national disaster management centre who appeal to Treasury Willem “ While this 127 million was being spent last year we started motivating and requesting further financial support for this area. Script” The declaration is for 3 months and then it must be renewed on a monthly basis, ideally until the drought ends. The Department of Agriculture estimates R450 million rand is needed for the first 3 months and its likely to escalate to R600 million. The fundamental problem is droughts are not finite, they require an open ended budget, until the rains come and the veld recovers, and that’s not happening Claire “Has the premier of the Northern Cape declared this a disaster area. Willem ” We as organised agriculture had a meeting with the Premier in the end of July 2019 and we made presentations to him. He listened to us he gave us a good ear...and since then nothing has happened. Claire “Nothing. Willem “ We haven't seen a provincial declaration and we haven't seen any aid yet Script” Finally on Friday deputy president David Mabusa visited the region and agreed the situation is dire. “National Government as well as the province will try and cooperate pull hands together and help the farmers Script “Committing to R30 million for immediate relief, with more to follow. Over the past year the Department of Agriculture has assisted with fodder where they could, but what keeps farmers spirits up are donations from the public Sybrand ” there are people who do huge work people like radio Tygerberg gave us a bunch of loads of of feed and on one day we could give 163 farmers each a bakkie of feed. So rain doesn’t always come out of the sky, rain sometimes comes down the tarred road as well Link “Even if it rained today and the drought relief funding arrived it would still take another five years for this community to begin to recover Sybrand ”To recover economically - You’re talking about long term loans people have taken on. It will take 10, 15, some guys 20 years just to work off that debt. But you have to go on because it’s in our blood, it’s our life, we just have to hang in there and to hope and believe Dirk “ My spirituality says to hold out, because I think God is aware of what is happening and we still believe there will be a solution. metadata.Unique Selling Point: The rains came for the rest of the drought stricken country but in the central Karoo, Carnarvon, Williston Sutherland the main sheep producing areas its been 7 long dry years. They got 3 months of drought relief in 2018 but the rains never came and the farmers cant go on. The biggest causality are the farm workers, half have been laid off. Emerging farmers can't afford to employ anyone permanently and rely on causal workers when they have enough money to employ them. People are surviving on SASA grants and soup kitchens. Kids are turning to crime and dropping out of school with drug and alcohol abuse is rife
metadata.Summary: In many parts of the country the drought has broken- the horrific images of the Free State KZN that haunted our lives- these farmers have had rain. But the area in the central Karoo around Carnarvon, Sutherland and Williston they are into their 7th year of drought. Sheep numbers decreased by 11 870, and average weaning percentage by 27%. The average feed bill per month is R52 461. The sheep are dying, the ewes are not lambing and the farmers are slaughtering their breeding stock because they can’t afford to feed them. The price of red meat has dropped by R10 kilogram n effect on a 20kg carcass the producer gets nearly R200 less per lamb. 12 000 less sheep from 26 farmers equals R2,4million loss. They have been waiting for over a year to get assistance from the State despite the area having been declared a disaster area in 2018.
metadata.Further information: There are 30 emerging farmers in the Carnarvon area and they are really battling. They rent land from the Municipality and they can’t afford the rent because productivity is down. Dirk Saccoo head of the Emerging Farmers Assocaition used to have 1000 sheep he now has 200. They can’t afford to employ people on a fulltime basis anymore so only take casual labour when they need something fixed. They can’t fix the fences because they don’t have money and the jackals are attacking and killing the sheep. They can’t get credit at the Agri Co-Op for feed or from the banks. They are also victim to stock left. Dirk is also on the security council so can speak to the other farmers problems. He cannot afford the petrol to drive to his farm which is 140 kms out of town- he used to make the trip twice a week now barley gets their once a week. The farm workers that are still on the farms are having to do everything on their own from repairing fences to feeding the sheep to fixing the windmills. The farmers can’t afford the fuel to travel back and forth so they have to survive longer and longer on their own managing the farms. Essentially it’s a humanitarian crisis- farmers are just not employing people on the farms- out of the 150 farms that would cover 300 families and on every farm they have has lost either 1 or 2 workers and when you consider they only employ 3 or 4 people that a huge impact. Usually farmers also used 6 casual workers on a day for big work, now they take only 2. There is no money for additional work like fence maintenance. Side line industries are failing and the people they employ. For example Sybrand Venter used to run a sideline business of scanning pregnant ewes he used to scan 35 000 ewes now if he scans 1000 it’s a lot. Danie Franken manager of the local Abattoir in Carnarvon says they employed 89 people- they are the largest employer in town. The number of sheep that are being slaughtered has fallen so dramatically that they are only working 4 days a week instead of 5. The abattoir used to slaughter 175 000 sheep in normal years, last year it’s down to 100 000, the expectation for this year is 80 000. They recently retrenched 10 workers and no longer employ casual workers- so 35 people have lost work. Each person supports on average 4 people so the impact here is on 140 people. In Williston they are already working short time so people are earning 80% of their wages Lamb sales are down by 50% because the economy is so bad as a result the price of red meat per kg has dropped by R10 kg so R200 less for every sheep. Imported lanb is selling at R37kg which the local market can just not compete against The farmers are slaughtering replacement ewes and even pregnant ewes just to survive. This means even if they do get some rain it will be a number of years before the stock can increase. The Local Spar and DIY and garage is owned by Heinz Germann- he reports an 42% drop in their turn over- farmers and workers cannot afford any treats or luxuries they are buying the essential. They used to employ 86 people between the 3 businesses and now only 50 people- 30 people have lost their jobs impacting 120 people. But all expenses have increased- Rates, electricity and insurance. 50% of the workers are now unemployed so people with young children are surviving on SASA grants from their kids. Many workers already returned to town when they lost their jobs on the farms that were bought up around SKA – this number has increased over the last few years- this is visually evident with the growing numbers of workers gathering in town on a Monday looking for casual work The social worker off the record says there is a growing problem with the kids, increasing housebreaking, drug and alcohol abuse, the children are neglected. For example she is dealing with an 11 years girl who old broke into a house and stole stuff. There is an increasing in crime and rape, with a growing problem of drug abuse but there has always been a problem of alcohol abuse. The school principle of the junior school - Vanessa Vyfer will go on camera- she says for many of the kids the only meal they eat is the one they get at school. The kids that used to stay in the hostel have moved out now that their parents are back in town, which she can’t understand because it’s not because of financial problems, they only pay R50 and if they can’t afford it she does make them pay. Sometimes they run a soup kitchen for the community when they have extra food and she says the queues of starving people is hectic. Willem Symington -Vice Chairman Agri Northern Cape. He works with the 3 spheres of Government to get drought relief, he is very articulate and comfortable speaking English and has a very good grip on where the blocks of access to funding lie. They have been trying to get funding since last July and with elections and new people appointed to positions basically every just stopped working until the new people were in place. In August this year they finally declared the area a disaster but it has to be registered in the Government gazette and it’s now September and that has not happened and the concern is that money has to be released within 3 months. The bigger picture is the agricultural disasters used to be handled by the DAFF but they are no longer- all disasters whether floods or drought are now handled by Co-operative governance, traditional affairs and Human Settlement- COGTHS- essentially it’s a mess and he spends his life traveling to Kimberly or De Aar to handle the various layers of Government to unlock the funding.
metadata.Extra Budget Items: Carnarvon is a 4 hour drive from Kimberley and then the farms are outside Carnarvon so approximately 10 hours of our 2 shoot days will be spent travelling. The flights are expensive so in order to get the content and quality images to justify the expense of the flights it makes sense to fly in on the Sunday evening. We also need a car with high clearance as we will be travelling on farm roads
